questions.text:
Based on the seven common characteristics of organisms, explain why mammals and
trees are living things. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Content Description Mark
Nutrition - Mammals carry out heterotrophic nutrition / feed
on other living organisms.
- Trees carry out autotrophic nutrition / make their
own food by photosynthesis.
Respiration - Mammals break down food in their cells to release
energy for body activities such as movement,
growth and repair.
- Trees break down food in their cells to release
energy for growth and development.
Excretion - Mammals excrete metabolic wastes in exhaled gas,
sweat and urine.
- Some trees store metabolic wastes in leaves which
are shed off.
Movement - Mammals move from place to place to search for
food, to find mates and to escape from danger.
- Trees move during growing: shoots grow towards
light and roots grow towards water.
Sensitivity - Mammals have sensory organs and muscular
systems to detect and respond to light, sound,
chemicals and many other stimuli.
- Trees can detect light and water, and grow towards
them.
Growth - Both mammals and trees grow by increasing their
body size and complexity.
Reproduction - In mammals, sperms and ova fuse to form zygotes
which will develop into offspring.
- In trees, the male gametes and female gametes fuse
to form embryos in seeds, which will germinate to
(Max. 7)
form new individuals.
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(10 marks)

questions.text:
There are different types of biomolecules in the human body. Each type has specific
functions in the human body. Describe how the structures of proteins and nucleic acids
are related to their functions. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Proteins (Max. 4)
 Proteins are long chains of polypeptides made up of amino acids joined by peptide
bonds. (1)
 The human body metabolizes proteins to release energy when lipids and
carbohydrates are in shortage. (1)
 Amino acids are deaminated in the liver. The remaining parts of amino acids are
changed into carbohydrates and lipids, which can be respired to release energy. (1)
 Protein molecules have specific 3D structure (conformation). (1)
 Enzymes are protein molecules which have a specific active site to bind to
substrate molecules. (1)
 Enzymes can speed up chemical reactions. (1)
 Antibodies are protein molecules which have specific binding site to the antigens
on pathogens. (1)
 Antibodies can produce immune response against pathogens. (1)
 Some hormones are protein molecules which have structures specific to the
receptors on target cells. (1)
 Hormones help to regulate different processes in the body. (1)
Nucleic acids (Max. 4)
 DNA and RNA are nucleic acids found in the human body. They consist of
numerous nucleotides joined together. (1)
 The base sequences in DNA molecules carry genetic information. (1)
 The double helix structure stabilizes DNA. (1)
 RNA is involved in protein synthesis. (1)
 The base sequence in RNA determines the amino acid sequence in a polypeptide
chain. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Discuss the significance of condensation and hydrolysis reactions to living organisms
using carbohydrates as an example. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
 The condensation of monosaccharides forms disaccharides or polysaccharides.
Water is produced in the process. (1)
 In hydrolysis, complex molecules are broken down into simpler molecules. Water
is utilized in the process. (1)
 The condensation of glucose and fructose produces sucrose which is the transport
form of sugars in plants. (1)
 The condensation of numerous glucose molecules produces cellulose, which is a
major component of the cell wall in plant cells. (1)
 The condensation of numerous glucose molecules produces starch, which acts as an
energy reserve in plants. (1)
 The condensation of numerous glucose molecules produces glycogen, which acts
as an energy reserve in animals. (1)
 Starch and glycogen can be hydrolysed to release glucose molecules to be used in
respiration to release energy. (1)
 When the blood glucose level is lower than normal, the glycogen stored in the liver
can be hydrolysed to release glucose molecules to restore a normal blood glucose
level. (1)
 Disaccharides and polysaccharides in ingested food are hydrolysed into
monosaccharides to be absorbed through the intestinal walls. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Both triglycerides and phospholipids are important lipids in the human body. Describe
the structural similarities and differences between triglycerides and phospholipids, and
explain their functions in the human body with appropriate examples. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Structural similarities and differences between triglycerides and phospholipids:
 Both a triglyceride molecule and a phospholipid molecule contain a glycerol
molecule. (1)
 A triglyceride molecule consists of three fatty acid molecules. (1)
 A phospholipid molecule consists of two fatty acid molecules and a phosphate
group. (1)
Functions of triglycerides and phospholipids in the human body:
 Triglycerides can be stored as energy reserves. (1)
 Adipose tissue under the skin (i.e. subcutaneous fat) acts as an insulating layer to
reduce heat loss. (1)
 Adipose tissues around internal organs act as shock-absorbers for protection. (1)
 Phospholipids are the main components of cell membranes (1)
 which controls the entry and exit of molecules into and out of the cell. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Some cells produce and secrete proteins (e.g. enzymes). Give an account of how
organelles work together for the production and secretion of proteins. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
 The nucleus commands (1)
ribosomes to synthesize proteins. (1)
 Many ribosomes are attached to endoplasmic reticulum which forms an extensive
network spanning across the cell. (1)
 The proteins synthesized by ribosomes are transported by the endoplasmic
reticulum. (1)
 Vesicles containing proteins are formed and they migrate towards the cell
membrane. (1)
 The vesicles fuse with the cell membrane. (1)
 The proteins inside the vesicles are released out of the cell by exocytosis. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(10 marks)

questions.text:
Bacteria are unicellular organisms. Each bacterial cell must carry out all of the vital
processes required for life. Explain which sub-cellular structures of a bacterial cell carry
out these vital processes. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
 The cell membrane allows the absorption of nutrients from the environment. (1)
 Some bacteria contain chlorophyll which allows photosynthesis to occur to
synthesize carbohydrates. (1)
 The cell membrane also controls the exit of substances from the cell, e.g. metabolic
wastes. (1)
 The cytoplasm contains enzymes which catalyse various metabolic reactions. (1)
 DNA controls all activities of the cell, such as protein synthesis and
reproduction. (1)
 Ribosomes synthesize proteins based on instructions from DNA. (1)
 Flagella can be used for locomotion/movement of the bacterial cell. (1)
 The cell wall protects the cell from damage / prevents the cell from bursting. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Give an account on the structure of proteins and their roles in the cell membrane.
(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Structure of proteins (Max. 3)
 Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide chain. (1)
 The polypeptide chain coils / folds up to form a helical or parallel structure. (1)
 The polypeptide chain may further coil and fold to form a three-dimensional
structure. (1)
 When more than one polypeptide chains bind together, they form a protein
molecule with specific conformation. (1)
Roles of proteins in the cell membrane (Max. 4)
 Proteins stabilize the membrane structure. (1)
 Channel proteins allow ions and water soluble substances to pass through. (1)
 Carrier proteins are involved in active transport. (1)
 Membrane-bound enzymes catalyse chemical reactions. (1)
 Glycoproteins may act as recognition markers. (1)
 Receptor proteins bind with specific hormones / messengers which stimulate or
inhibit certain cellular activities. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(10 marks)

questions.text: Discuss osmosis and its importance to organisms. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Definition of osmosis
 Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water
potential to a region of lower water potential across a differentially permeable
membrane (1)
Effects of osmosis to cells
 When plant cells are bathed in a hypotonic solution, the cells gain water and
become turgid. (1)
 When plant cells are bathed in a hypertonic solution, the cells lose water and
become plasmolysed. (1)
 When animal cells are bathed in a hypotonic solution, the cells gain water and lyse
(e.g. haemolysis). (1)
 When animal cells are bathed in a hypertonic solution, the cells lose water and
shrink. (1)
Importance to organisms (Max. 4)
 Animals:
- Water in the lumen of the intestines is absorbed by osmosis. (1)
- Water in the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed by osmosis. By adjusting the
permeability of the kidney tubules to water, the amount of water excreted in
urine can be controlled. (1)
 Plants:
- Water in the soil is absorbed into the roots by osmosis. (1)
- Plant cells gain water by osmosis and become turgid. Turgidity gives support
to plants. (1)
 Daily lives:
- Humans make use of the principle of osmosis to preserve food by soaking
food in concentrated sugar or salt solution. (1)
- Humans make use of the principle of osmosis to design dialysis machines for
haemodialysis for patients with kidney failure. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text: Account for the factors that affect the rate of enzymatic reactions. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Content Description Mark
Temperature - At low temperatures, most enzymes are inactive.
- As the temperature rises, the substrate and enzyme
molecules have more kinetic energy and move
faster. The substrate and enzyme molecules collide
with one another and enzyme-substrate complexes
are more likely to form.
- The rate of an enzymatic reaction reaches its
maximum at the optimum temperature.
- When the temperature increases beyond the
optimum temperature, the shapes of the active sites
of the enzymes start to change.
- Enzymes are denatured at very high temperatures.
- The loss of catalytic function of enzymes at high
temperatures is irreversible. (Max. 4)
pH - Enzymes work best at their optimum pH.
- A change in pH alters the shape of the enzyme
molecules and their active sites.
- Most enzymes are denatured at extreme pH values.
Inhibitors - Inhibitors (e.g. cyanide, heavy metal ions) bind to
enzymes and decrease the rate of enzymatic
reactions.
Enzyme and - The higher the substrate concentration, the higher is
substrate the reaction rate until the rate of reaction is limited
concentration by the enzyme concentration.
- When the rate of reaction is limited by the enzyme
concentration, the rate of reaction can be increased
if more enzyme molecules are added. (Max. 5)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Protein is an important food substance for humans. Either insufficient or excess intake
of protein could cause undesirable effects to humans. Discuss the functions of proteins
in humans and the undesirable effects may be caused if protein consumption are
insufficient and in excess respectively. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Functions of proteins (Max. 3)
 As the components of various cellular structures (1)
 Involved in forming new cells for growth and repair (1)
 Form enzymes, antibodies and some hormones (1)
 As a source of energy when the body is short of carbohydrates and lipids (1)
Insufficient intake of protein (Max. 2)
 The body will break down proteins, especially those in muscles, to release energy,
(1)
leading to muscle loss. (1)
 Severe protein deficiency can lead to kwashiorkor (1)
which causes stunted growth / anaemia / hair loss / the accumulation of tissue fluid
in the abdomen. (1)
Excess intake of protein (Max. 2)
 Excess amino acids are broken down in the liver by deamination. (1)
 Eating too much protein over a long period of time would cause the liver to
become overloaded, (1)
leading to liver damage. (1)
 Excess protein intake would cause weight gain. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(10 marks)

questions.text:
Some people adopt a vegetarian diet for its health benefits. Some people argue that
adopting a vegetarian diet cannot obtain the right proportions of all the essential food
substances that the human body needs. Discuss the benefits of a vegetarian diet and
explain how vegetarians can maintain a balanced diet. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Benefits of a vegetarian diet
 A vegetarian diet is based on plant foods which are usually rich in dietary fibre.
Obtaining enough dietary fibre can maintain normal peristalsis / prevent
constipation. (1)
 Fresh fruit and vegetables usually have high vitamin C content. Obtaining enough
vitamin C can prevent scurvy / help the healing of wounds / maintain healthy gums,
teeth and skin. (1)
 A vegetarian diet usually contains not much lipid. This can help with weight
control / prevent obesity. (1)
How vegetarians can maintain a balanced diet
 A well-planned vegetarian diet is a balanced diet. When planning a vegetarian diet,
extra attention should be paid to ensure the diet includes sufficient amount of
proteins, calcium, iron and vitamin B12. (1)
 Proteins can be obtained from eggs, nuts, legumes and soya products. (1)
 Calcium can be obtained from dairy products, tofu, calcium-fortified soya milk and
green leafy vegetables. (1)
 Iron can be obtained from beans, tofu, spinach and some seeds such as pumpkin
seeds and sesame seeds. (1)
 Vitamin B12 can be obtained from eggs, fortified soya milk and cereals. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
In developing countries, an estimated 146 million children suffer from stunted growth
due to severe malnutrition. Give an account of the likely effects of long-term severe
malnutrition, other than on growth, on the body of a young child. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Effects of severe malnutrition (Max. 4)
 Low intakes of carbohydrates and fats lead to a decrease in glycogen and fat stores
/ severe weight loss / muscle wasting / weak muscle. (1)
 A lack of proteins leads to kwashiorkor. (1)
 Fewer enzymes / hormones / antibodies are produced, affecting metabolism and
immunity. (1)
 Water potential of blood plasma increases, leading to the accumulation of tissue
fluid in organs / abdomen. (1)
Effects of vitamin or mineral deficiencies (Max. 3)
 Deficiency of vitamin A leads to night blindness. (1)
 Deficiency of vitamin D leads to rickets / poor absorption of calcium. (1)
 Deficiency of vitamin C leads to scurvy. (1)
 Deficiency of iron leads to anaemia. (1)
 Deficiency of calcium leads to rickets / tooth decay. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(10 marks)

questions.text: Discuss the importance of vitamins and minerals to our bodies. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Importance of vitamins (Max. 4)
 Vitamin A is important for the formation of visual purple in the retina. (1)
It can keep the cornea of the eyes, the skin, and the lining of the alimentary canal
and the respiratory system healthy. (1)
 A deficiency of vitamin A may cause night blindness / thickening of the cornea /
dry skin and an increased risk of infection of the lining of the respiratory system. (1)
 Vitamin C is important for the formation of connective tissues. (1)
It also helps wound healing and maintains healthy gums, teeth and skin. (1)
 A deficiency of vitamin C may cause scurvy. (1)
 Vitamin D helps the absorption of calcium and phosphate ions from the intestine.
(1)
 A deficiency of vitamin D may cause rickets and osteoporosis. (1)
Importance of minerals (Max. 3)
 Calcium is important for the formation of bones and teeth, (1)
for blood clotting and muscle contraction. (1)
 A deficiency of calcium may cause rickets and osteoporosis. (1)
 Iron is needed in the formation of haemoglobin. (1)
 A deficiency of iron may cause anaemia. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(10 marks)

questions.text:
Nitrogen is a mineral essential to the human body. Give an account on how humans
obtain nitrogen from diet and the assimilation of nitrogen into body proteins. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Source of nitrogen
 Humans obtain nitrogen from proteins in food. (1)
Digestion of proteins in food
 Food containing proteins is mechanically broken into small pieces in the mouth
cavity and the stomach (chewing by the teeth and churning in the stomach) (1)
 Chemical digestion of proteins starts in the stomach. Gastric juice contains
proteases and hydrochloric acid. (1)
 The protease pepsin in the stomach catalyses the breakdown of proteins into
peptides. (1)
 In the small intestine, pancreatic proteases catalyse the breakdown of proteins into
peptides and amino acids. (1)
 Proteases on the cell membranes of the epithelial cells in the intestinal wall
catalyse the breakdown of peptides into amino acids. (1)
Absorption of amino acids
 Amino acids in the small intestine are absorbed by diffusion and active transport
into the blood capillaries of the villi. (1)
 The amino acids are carried by the bloodstream to different parts of the body for
cells to use. (1)
Assimilation of amino acids
 Amino acids are used as raw material to make organelles (e.g. cell membrane and
cytoplasm), cells, muscles, connective tissue, etc. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
John ate some fried pork chops at dinner. Discuss how the lipids in the pork chops are
digested and absorbed, and how the lipids may become his body fat. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Digestion of lipids (Max. 3)
 In the duodenum, bile and pancreatic juice help the digestion of lipids. (1)
 Bile, which is secreted by the liver, contains bile salts. (1)
 Bile salts cause the emulsification of lipids into smaller droplets. (1)
 Pancreatic juice, which is secreted by the pancreas, contains pancreatic lipase. (1)
 The small oil droplets are digested by pancreatic lipase into fatty acids and
glycerol. (1)
 Digestion of lipids is optimum under alkaline condition. (1)
Absorption of fatty acids and glycerol (Max. 3)
 Fatty acids and glycerol molecules pass through the epithelium of the villi by
diffusion (1)
 and then recombine to form lipid molecules (1)
 which then enter the lacteal (1)
 and are carried away by the lymph. (1)
Assimilation of lipids (Max. 3)
 After entering the lacteal, lipid molecules are carried by the lymph through the
lymph vessels. (1)
 The lymph vessels eventually open into two large veins near the neck region,
returning lymph to the blood. (1)
 The lipid molecules are carried by the bloodstream to different parts of the body
and are taken up by cells for metabolism. (1)
 Excess lipid molecules are stored as adipose tissues around internal organs or
subcutaneous fat under the skin. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Describe how the structure of different parts of the alimentary canal, starting from the
stomach, enables humans to perform digestion and absorption (details of the enzyme
reactions are not required). (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Alimentary canal
 The whole alimentary canal is made up of circular muscles and longitudinal
muscles. (1)
 Alternate contraction and relaxation of these two layers of muscles enables
peristalsis. (1)
Stomach (max. 2)
 The stomach is a muscular sac. (1)
 It can expand to accommodate variable amounts of food. (1)
 Gastric glands in the inner wall of the stomach secrete gastric juice for the
digestion of proteins. (1)
 The muscular wall of the stomach contracts rhythmically (called churning).
Churning helps break food into smaller pieces and mix food with gastric juice. (1)
Small intestine (max. 4)
 The membranes of epithelial cells of the small intestine contain carbohydrases and
proteases for the digestion of disaccharides and peptides. (1)
 The small intestine is very long. (1)
 The inner surface of the small intestine is highly-folded / contains many villi and
microvilli. (1)
 This increases the surface area for absorption. (1)
 The epithelium of each villus is thin / one-cell thick. (1)
 This shortens the distance of absorption. (1)
 Each villus contains a network of capillaries and a lacteal. (1)
 This enables rapid absorption / transport of digested food molecules. (1)
 The inner surface of the small intestine secretes mucus (1)
 for lubrication /ease of passage of food / preventing self-digestion. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
The ileum is an organ. In complex organisms, cells are organized into tissues which are
organized into organs. Based on your biological knowledge, discuss the roles of the
different tissue layers of the ileum in digestion and absorption. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Epithelium of the inner wall of the ileum (Max. 4)
 It is the innermost layer which is in contact with food. (1)
 It is deeply folded into numerous villi to increase the surface area for
absorption. (1)
 The surface of the epithelial cells of villi bears microvilli which further increases
the surface area for absorption. (1)
 The epithelium of each villus is thin / one-cell thick. This shortens the distance of
absorption. (1)
 The epithelial cells of villi contain many mitochondria which provide energy for
active transport of certain food molecules. (1)
Blood vessels and lymph vessels (Max. 2)
 The blood vessels branch into many networks of blood capillaries, while the lymph
vessels branch into many lacteals. (1)
 Each villus has a central lacteal surrounded by a dense network of capillaries.
These vessels carry the absorbed nutrients away rapidly. (1)
Circular muscles and longitudinal muscles (Max. 2)
 Alternate contraction and relaxation of these two layers of muscles enables
peristalsis. (1)
 Peristalsis moves food along the ileum. (1)
 Peristalsis helps mix food and digestive juice together. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Describe and explain how oxygen in the atmospheric air passes into the lungs of humans
and how it is absorbed into the blood. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Oxygen is brought to the air sacs by inhalation (Max. 4)
The intercostal muscles contract, and the rib cage moves upwards and outwards. (1)
⚫
The diaphragm muscles contract, and the diaphragm becomes flattened. (1)
⚫
The thoracic volume increases and the lungs expand. (1)
⚫
The air pressure in the lungs becomes lower than the atmospheric pressure. (1)
⚫
Atmospheric air, which contains a higher concentration of oxygen, is drawn into
⚫
lungs. (1)
Gas exchange in the air sacs (Max. 4)
In the air sacs of the lungs, oxygen in the incoming air dissolves in the water film on
⚫
the inner surface of the air sacs. (1)
As the oxygen concentration of the water film is higher than the blood of the
⚫
capillaries, (1)
oxygen diffuses across the walls of the air sacs and capillaries into the blood. (1)
Oxygen then diffuses into red blood cells (1)
⚫
and combines with haemoglobin in the red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Describe how carbon dioxide is transported from a body cell to an air sac in the lungs
and then removed by the lungs. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Transport of carbon dioxide from the body cells to the lungs (Max. 3)
Carbon dioxide is formed in body cells during respiration. (1)
⚫
Carbon dioxide diffuses into the blood along the concentration gradient. (1)
⚫
Most carbon dioxide enters the red blood cells and reacts readily with water to form
⚫
hydrogencarbonate ions. (1)
The ions diffuse out of the red blood cells and dissolve in the blood plasma. (1)
⚫
Blood is then transported back to the heart via venae cavae and is then pumped to
⚫
the lungs via the pulmonary artery. (1)
(Or other acceptable answers)
Gas exchange in the air sacs (Max. 2)
The carbon dioxide concentration in the air sacs is lower than that in the blood. (1)
⚫
When the blood reaches the lungs, hydrogencarbonate ions enter the red blood cells
⚫
and break down to form carbon dioxide and water. (1)
Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood plasma into the air of an air sac. (1)
⚫
Removal of carbon dioxide from the lungs by exhalation (Max. 4)
The intercostal muscles relax, and the rib cage moves downwards and inwards. (1)
⚫
The diaphragm muscles relax, and the diaphragm returns to dome-shaped. (1)
⚫
The thoracic volume and lung volume decrease. (1)
⚫
The air pressure in the lungs becomes higher than the atmospheric pressure. (1)
⚫
Air in the air sacs, which contains a higher concentration of carbon dioxide, is
⚫
forced out of the lungs. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Describe how lymph is formed and how it can be returned to the blood circulation.
(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Formation of lymph (Max. 6)
At the arterial end of the capillary bed, the hydrostatic pressure of the blood is
⚫
higher than the tissue fluid. (1)
Some components of the plasma (e.g. water, minerals, glucose and amino acids) (1)
⚫
are forced out through the differentially permeable capillary walls to become tissue
fluid. (1)
Plasma proteins, red blood cells and blood platelets and remain in the blood due to
⚫
their large sizes. (1)
At the venous end of the capillary bed, water moves into the capillary bed by
⚫
osmosis. (1)
Excess tissue fluid will enter the lymph capillaries to form lymph (1)
⚫
due to the higher hydrostatic pressure in the body tissues. (1)
Return of lymph to the heart (Max. 3)
The contraction of skeletal muscles adjacent to the lymph vessels pushes the lymph
⚫
forward. (1)
The presence of valves in lymph vessels prevents the backflow of lymph. (1)
⚫
During inhalation, the decrease in pressure of the thoracic cavity helps draw the
⚫
lymph towards the heart. (1)
The large lymph vessels join two large veins at the base of the neck, where the
⚫
lymph returns to the blood circulation. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________

questions.text:

questions.text:
Both humans and plants develop vascular system(s) for transport within their bodies.
Contrast the structure of their vascular systems. Explain why transport in human is
more effective than that in plants. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Structures of their vascular systems: (Max. 4)
 Humans have two connected systems―the lymphatic system opens into the blood
circulation, while plants have two separate systems―xylem and phloem. (1)
 The blood vessels and lymph vessels in humans are made up of living cells. In
plants, xylem is made up of dead cells and phloem is made up of living cells. (1)
 The lumens of vessels in humans are surrounded by cells (extracellular), while the
lumens of vessels in plants are within cells (intracellular). (1)
 The diameter of vessels in humans can be adjusted (arteries are elastic / veins can
be distended), while vessels in plants are rigid and their diameter is fixed. (1)
 Valves are present in veins and lymph vessels of humans, while sieve plates are
present in the phloem of plants. (1)
Why transport in humans is more effective: (Max. 4)
 In humans, the heart acts as a pump to provide the driving force to propel blood
along vessels, while there is no well defined organ to generate a driving force in
plants. (1)
 In humans, the continuous flow of blood and lymph are maintained by various
ways:
- the elastic wall of arteries recoils and pushes blood forward (1)
- presence of valves in veins and lymph vessels to prevent backflow (1)
- contraction of skeletal muscle squeezes lymph and venous blood towards the
heart (1)
- inhalation creates a negative pressure in the thorax to draw in lymph and
venous blood from the peripheral circulation (1)
while transpiration pull and root pressure in plants provide the driving force to
maintain the flow. (1)

questions.text:
Explain how plants absorb water from roots and then transport it to the leaf.
(11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Content Description Mark
Water - Soil water usually has a water potential higher than
absorption that of the cytoplasm and the cell sap of the root hair
cells.
- Water therefore moves into the root hair by osmosis.
- Water moves across the cortex from cell to cell by
osmosis until it reaches the xylem vessels.
- Some water may move inwards along the cell walls,
from cell to cell, without entering the cytoplasm or the
vacuole.
- Eventually, water is drawn up the xylem vessels by the
transpiration pull. (Max. 4)
Water - In the leaves, water evaporates from the surface of
transport mesophyll cells through the stomata by transpiration.
- Water is continuously drawn from neighbouring cells
to replace the water lost.
- Eventually, water is drawn from the xylem vessels.
- A water potential gradient is generated, causing water
to flow from the xylem through leaf cells to replace the
water loss.
- Due to the surface tension of water, a force
(transpiration pull) is produced which pulls water up
the xylem vessels from the root. (Max. 4)
Communication (Max. 3)

questions.text:
Describe the events that occur during one complete cell cycle in an animal cell.
(13 marks)
questions.answerText:
Interphase (Max. 3)
During interphase, the cell carries out the following activities to prepare for the next cell
division: (1)
- DNA replication (1)
- Synthesis of proteins (1)
- Synthesis of new organelles (1)
Mitotic cell division (Max. 7)
- Prophase: The chromatin / replicated DNA coils up tightly into chromosomes. (1)
The nuclear membrane disappears. (1)
- Metaphase: The chromosomes line up along the equatorial plane. (1)
Spindle fibres attach to the chromosomes at the centromeres. (1)
- Anaphase: The spindle fibres shorten and pull the sister chromatids of each
chromosomes towards the opposite poles of the cell. (1)
- Telophase: A nuclear membrane forms around each group of daughter
chromosomes. (1)
The chromosomes loosen to become chromatin again. (1)
- Cytokinesis: The cell membrane around the middle of the dividing cell constricts to
form a cleavage furrow. The furrow further deepens to divide the cytoplasm into
two halves. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)

(13 marks)

questions.text: Discuss meiotic cell division and its importance to organisms. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Content Descriptor Marks
1. Introduction - It is a kind of cell division which involves two
of meiotic successive divisions: meiosis I and meiosis II.
cell division - It is found in the gamete-producing cells found in
the sex organs (e.g. anthers and ovaries in
flowering plants; testis and ovaries in animals).
- In meiosis, pairs of homologous chromosomes line
up and arrange themselves randomly in the middle
of the cell.
- Each homologous chromosomes pair separates
independently and moves to opposite pole of cells.
- Each cell produces four haploid cells per meiosis. (Max. 4)
2. Importance to - It forms haploid gametes in organisms for sexual
organisms reproduction by halving the chromosome number.
- The independent assortment and crossing over of

questions.text:
Describe how flowering plants can reproduce sexually by means of flowers and seeds.
(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Content Description Mark
Pollination - Male gametes are produced in the anthers by
meiotic cell division.
- Male gametes are carried by pollen grains.
- Pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the
stigma by means of insects / wind / external
agents. (Max. 2)
Fertilization - When a pollen grain lands on the stigma, the
sugary solution secreted by the stigma stimulates
the pollen grain to develop a pollen tube.
- The pollen tube secretes enzymes to digest the
tissues of the carpel, and grows down through the
style and the ovary.
- The pollen tube then enters the micropyle and
releases the male gamete.
- The male gamete then fuses with the female
gamete to form a zygote. (Max. 3)
Development of - After fertilization, the ovary gradually develops
fruits and seeds into a fruit.
- The zygote develops into the embryo.
- The ovule develops into the seed.
- Integuments develop into the seed coat.
- The ovary wall develops into the fruit wall. (Max. 2)
Development of - The fruits / seeds are dispersed by wind / animal /
a new plant water / other reasonable answer.
- Under favourable conditions (e.g. optimum
temperature, with adequate water), the seeds
germinate.
- The embryo in the seed uses the food reserves in
cotyledons to develop into a new plant. (Max. 2)

questions.text: Outline the process from sperm production to fertilization. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:

Sperm - In the testis, cells in the walls of the seminiferous

- Newly-formed sperms are temporarily stored in

fluid. (1)

Cowper’s glands and prostate glands. Sperms are

- When a male is sexually excited, the normally
soft penis becomes erect and hard. (1)
- During sexual intercourse, the erect penis of the
male is inserted into the vagina of the female. (1)
- Semen is ejaculated from the penis into the
vagina near the cervix. (1) (Max. 3)
Fertilization - Sperms swim through the cervix, the uterus and
into the oviducts. (1)
- Sperms meet an ovum in the oviduct. (1)
- A sperm penetrates the ovum by releasing

questions.text:
Give an account on how the pancreas is involved in the rise of the blood glucose level
after a carbohydrate-rich meal and the related homeostatic control. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Rise in the blood glucose level after a carbohydrate-rich meal (4)
 The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice to the duodenum through the
pancreatic duct. (1)
 Pancreatic juice contains pancreatic amylase which catalyses the breakdown of
starch in the chyme to maltose. (1)
 Maltose is then further broken down into glucose in the small intestine. (1)
 A lot of glucose is absorbed into the bloodstream from the small intestine; hence
the blood glucose level increases. (1)
Regulation of the blood glucose level (Max. 4)
 A rise in the blood glucose level is detected by the pancreas. (1)
 In response, the pancreas secretes more insulin and less glucagon into the blood. (1)
 Insulin stimulates the liver cells to convert excess glucose to glycogen. The
glycogen is then stored in the liver and muscles. (1)
 Insulin also stimulates the uptake of glucose by body cells and subsequent
oxidation of glucose by respiration. (1)
 As a result, the blood glucose level falls and returns to normal. (1)

questions.text:
State the different components of the negative feedback mechanism in the regulation of
blood glucose level and explain how the blood glucose level is regulated in humans.
(11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Main components of negative feedback mechanism in the regulation of blood glucose
level (Max. 3)
 Receptor: pancreas (1)
 Control centre: pancreas (1)
 Effector: liver cells / body cells (1)
When blood glucose level is higher than normal (Max. 3)
 The pancreas detects a rise in the blood glucose level. (1)
 It secretes more insulin and less glucagon into the blood. (1)
 Insulin stimulates the liver cells to convert excess glucose to glycogen. (1)
 Insulin stimulates the uptake of glucose by body cells and the subsequent oxidation
of glucose by respiration. (1)
 As a result, the blood glucose level falls and returns to normal.
When blood glucose level is lower than normal (Max. 2)
 The pancreas detects a fall in the blood glucose level. (1)
 It secretes more glucagon and less insulin into the blood. (1)
 Glucagon stimulates the liver cells to convert glycogen to glucose. (1)
 As a result, the blood glucose level rises and returns to normal.
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Give a brief account on how energy from the Sun is transferred and eventually used by a
person to move his/her arms. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Energy transfer from the Sun to a person (Max. 4)
 Sun light is captured by chlorophyll in plant cells to carry out photosynthesis. (1)
 The light energy is converted to chemical energy / energy stored in organic
molecules (e.g. glucose). (1)
 Plant material is consumed by consumers. (1)
 Consumers digest and metabolize the ingested plant material, thus incorporating
food substances from plants into their body tissues. (1)
 The chemical energy stored in plants is transferred along the food chain. (1)
 When a person consumes plants / consumers, he/she obtains the chemical energy
stored in the organic molecules in food. (1)
Release of energy from food to power movement (Max. 4)
 Organic molecules in food are digested by digestive enzymes in the
human body. (1)
 The digested food substances are absorbed in the small intestine and transported to
other parts of the body through the bloodstream. (1)
 Muscle cells take up the digested food substances / glucose from the blood. (1)
 Muscle cells carry out respiration to break down glucose, (1)
 which releases energy for the contraction of arm muscles. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Describe how the nitrogen in the protein of a cow may be transferred and incorporated
into the protein of a goat living in the same habitat. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Transfer of nitrogen from a cow to plants (Max. 4)
 The dead body of a cow / Organic waste expelled by a living cow is broken down
by fungi and putrefying bacteria. (1)
 The nitrogen in these organic materials is converted to ammonium compounds. (1)
 Under aerobic conditions, the ammonium compounds in the soil are oxidized by
nitrifying bacteria to nitrites and then to nitrates. (1)
 Nitrates are absorbed by plants / grasses through their roots. (1)
 Plants / Grasses use nitrates and the intermediates of photosynthesis to form
proteins. (1)
Transfer of nitrogen from plants to a goat (Max. 4)
 A goat ingests grasses that contain proteins. (1)
 Proteins from the grasses are digested by proteases in the goat’s digestive system
into amino acids. (1)
 The amino acids are absorbed in the intestines and transported by blood. (1)
 Body cells take up amino acids by diffusion and active transport. (1)
 Body cells synthesize proteins using the amino acids. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Describe how you would measure three different abiotic factors of a mangrove forest.
Further describe how each of these abiotic factors in the ecosystem could adversely
affect mangrove plants and explain how the plants have adapted to these conditions.
(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Measuring abiotic factors
 The oxygen concentration in coastal waters can be measured with a dissolved
oxygen meter. (1)
 The salinity of coastal waters can be measured with a refractometer. (1)
 The atmospheric temperature can be measured with a thermometer / a temperature
sensor connected to a data logger. (1)
Local effects of abiotic factors on mangrove plants
 The soil in mangrove forests are constantly waterlogged and thus poorly aerated,
which limits the mangrove plants’ oxygen uptake for respiration. (1)
 Mangrove plants are often immersed in saltwater, which could upset the plants’
osmotic balance. (1)
 The relatively high temperatures in the ecosystem increase the rate of transpiration
in the mangrove plants and may cause desiccation. (1)
Adaptations to the local effects of abiotic factors (Max. 3)
 Mangrove plants grow aerial roots / knee roots that rise above sea level to carry out
gas exchange regardless of tide levels. (1)
 Mangrove plants grow lenticels to maximize gas exchange. (1)
 Salt glands on the leaves of certain mangrove plants excrete excess salt, thereby
maintaining osmotic balance in the plant. (1)
 Certain mangrove plants have roots that are highly impermeable to salt, thereby
maintaining osmotic balance in the plant. (1)
 Mangrove plants generally have thick, waxy cuticles in their leaves to reduce water
loss due to transpiration. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Green plants are autotrophs while humans are heterotrophs.
Compare how green plants and humans obtain carbohydrates, transport these molecules
in their bodies and store them as energy reserve. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
How green plants and humans obtain carbohydrates: (Max. 2)
 Green plants can capture light energy and synthesize glucose using carbon dioxide
and water. (1)
 Green plants can use the glucose formed from photosynthesis to make other types
of carbohydrates such as sucrose, starch and cellulose. (1)
 Humans can obtain carbohydrates from organic food. Complex carbohydrates (e.g.
starch) in ingested food are digested into simple monosaccharides (e.g. glucose) for
absorption. (1)
How green plants and humans transport carbohydrates in their bodies: (Max. 4)
 In plants, carbohydrates are transported in the form of sucrose. (1)
 Sucrose is transported from the leaves to other parts of the plants (e.g. roots, fruits
and storage organs) through the phloem tissue. (1)
 Sucrose can also be transported from storage organs to the leaves and other
growing regions. (1)
 The transport of sucrose through the phloem is multidirectional. (1)
 After carbohydrates are digested in the human body, monosaccharides are absorbed
into the blood and transported by blood to various parts of the body. (1)
 Blood flow is maintained by the pumping action of the heart. (1)
 Blood flows in a branching network of blood vessels and circulates unidirectionally
from the heart in a specific route and returns to the heart again. (1)
Storage of carbohydrates as energy reserve: (Max. 2)
 In plants, carbohydrates are often stored in the form of starch (1)
in the stems, roots and underground storage organs. (1)
 In the human body, carbohydrates are often stored in the form of glycogen (1)
in muscles and the liver. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Discuss how the structure of a dicotyledonous green leaf is related to certain vital
functions of the plants. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
The leaves of a plant are the main sites of gas exchange and photosynthesis. (1)
Adaptations of the leaves for gas exchange and photosynthesis: (Max. 8)
 Leaves are usually broad and flat. (1)
This provides a large surface area for the exchange of gases and for absorbing light.
(1)
 The leaf blade is supported by the midrib and veins so that it spreads out to
maximize the surface area exposed to sunlight. (1)
 Leaves are thin. (1)
This shortens the distance for light and gases to reach the mesophyll cells. (1)
 The cuticle and epidermis are transparent so that light can penetrate and reach the
photosynthetic mesophyll beneath them. (1)
 The presence of stomata in the epidermis allows gases to pass into and out of the
leaves. (1)
 The guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata, thus regulating the rate
of gas exchange. (1)
When light is not available for photosynthesis, the stomata close to reduce the loss
of water vapour from the leaves. (1)
 The palisade mesophyll is located in the upper part of a leaf, facing the Sun
directly. The cells are closely packed and contain numerous chloroplasts. (1)
These help maximize the amount of light absorbed for photosynthesis. (1)
 The spongy mesophyll cells are loosely packed, with lots of air spaces among them.
This allows gases to diffuse freely inside the leaves. (1)
 A film of water is present on the surface of spongy mesophyll cells. Gases can first
dissolve in it and readily diffuse into the cells. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
With reference to the main stages of photosynthesis, explain what factors limit the rate
of photosynthesis. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Photochemical reactions: (Max. 3)
 Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and its electrons are excited to a higher
energy level. (1)
 As electrons pass through a series of electron carriers, energy is released. (1)
 The energy released is used to synthesize ATP through photophosphorylation. (1)
 The energy released is also used to split water molecules into oxygen and
hydrogen. (1)
 Hydrogen ions combine with NADP, forming NADPH. (1)
The rate of photochemical reactions is limited by low light intensity. Less ATP and
NADPH can be produced and enter the Calvin cycle. (1#)
The Calvin cycle: (Max. 3)
 Carbon dioxide combines with a 5-C carbon dioxide acceptor, forming two
molecules of a 3-C compound. (1)
 The 3-C compound is reduced by NADPH, forming triose phosphate. (1)
 For every 12 molecules of triose phosphate formed, two of which is used to form a
glucose molecule. (1)
 The remaining triose phosphate is used to regenerate the 5-C carbon dioxide
acceptor so that the cycle can repeat. (1)
The rate of the Calvin cycle is limited by low light intensity, because it requires ATP and
NADPH from the photochemical reactions. (1#)
The rate of the Calvin cycle is also limited by low concentration of carbon dioxide.
Fewer 3-C compounds can be formed from carbon dioxide fixtion and enter the Calvin
cycle. (1)
Temperature is a limiting factor of photosynthesis because many reactions are catalysed
by enzymes. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
# Marks should be awarded once only.
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
John participates in a 100 m race at his school’s Sports Day. Before the race, he drank a
glucose-rich drink. Describe how glucose from the drink can be supplied to John’s leg
muscles to fuel his running. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Journey of glucose from John’s alimentary canal to his leg muscles: (Max. 3)
 After the glucose-rich drink is swallowed, peristalsis of the alimentary canal moves
the glucose from the oesophagus to the small intestine. (1)
 In the small intestine, glucose is absorbed into the blood capillaries inside villi by
diffusion and active transport. (1)
 Glucose is carried by the blood and circulates around the body. (1)
 At the leg muscles, glucose diffuses from the blood to the muscle cells down the
concentration gradient as glucose is constantly consumed by the cells. (1)
Leg muscles use glucose to release energy aerobically and anaerobically: (Max. 4)
 During vigorous exercise such as a 100 m sprint, leg muscles cannot obtain enough
oxygen for aerobic respiration. The muscles carry out aerobic and anaerobic
respiration at the same time. (1)
 In aerobic respiration, each molecule of glucose is completely broken down
through glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative
phosphorylation (1)
with a yield of 38 molecules of ATP. (1)
 In anaerobic respiration, glucose goes through glycolysis only and is converted to
pyruvate which enters the anaerobic pathway. (1)
 Without oxygen, NADH transfers its hydrogen to pyruvate, which is then reduced
to lactic acid. NAD is regenerated to accept hydrogen in glycolysis once again. (1)
 The net ATP yield of anaerobic respiration in muscle cells is two molecules of ATP
from glycolysis. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(10 marks)

questions.text:
Photosynthesis and respiration are two important processes that support life. Describe
how green plants convert light energy from the Sun to chemical energy in organic food,
and how the green plants release energy in the form of ATP from organic food for
cellular activities. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
From light energy to chemical energy in organic food: (Max. 4)
 Green plants require light energy, carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and
oxygen. (1)
 Photosynthesis occurs in two stages. In photochemical reactions, light energy
captured by chlorophyll molecules drive photophosphorylation and photolysis of
water. (1)
Photophosphorylation synthesizes ATP from ADP and phosphate, while photolysis
of water produces NADPH and oxygen. (1)
 In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide combines with a 5-C carbon dioxide acceptor to
form two molecules of a 3-C compound. The 3-C compound is reduced to triose
phosphate. (1)
Some of the triose phosphate formed is synthesized into glucose. Glucose may be
used in respiration to release energy. (1)
Conversion of chemical energy in organic food to chemical energy in ATP: (Max. 4)
 In the presence of oxygen, glucose can be completely broken down to release
energy. Photosynthesis can supply oxygen and glucose for respiration. (1)
 Glucose is broken down into triose phosphate and then pyruvate in glycolysis.
Glycolysis synthesizes two molecules of ATP from one glucose molecule. (1)
 Pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA in the link reaction, with the release of carbon
dioxide. Acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle. (1)
 The Krebs cycle produces ATP, NADH, FADH and carbon dioxide. (1)
 When electrons from hydrogen atoms of NADH and FADH pass through a series
of electron carriers in the inner membrane of mitochondrion, energy is released to
phosphorylate ADP to ATP. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Since the 1950s, the number of deaths due to infectious diseases has been in decline in
developed countries. Explain such decline with regard to improvements on disease
prevention and treatment. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Prevention of disease: (Max. 5)
 Doctors and scientists have gained deeper understanding about the transmission
routes of pathogens. (1) This allows people to take measures to break the
transmission link and thus control the spread of the pathogens. (1)
 Improved personal hygiene, proper treatment of drinking water and proper food
processing and storage have reduced the risk of food and water contaminated with
pathogens. (1)
 Proper sewage treatment has prevented the spread of pathogens from human wastes
to the environment / water systems. (1)
 Improved environmental hygiene helps control the breeding of disease vectors such
as rats and mosquitoes. (1) This also reduces the survival of pathogens in the
environment. (1)
 Immunization programmes allow young children to have developed immunity
against common infectious disease such as polio and measles. (1) Thus the number
of infected persons in the community is reduced and so is the chance of disease
transmission. (1)
Treatment of diseases: (Max. 4)
 Different types of antibiotics and antiviral drugs have been discovered and mass
produced. (1) The drugs can quickly and effectively kill the pathogens in patients,
thus reducing the death rate. (1)
 Advancements in diagnostic techniques allow quick and accurate identification of
the causative agents, (1) thus treatment methods can target at the concerning
pathogens. (1) The recovery time is shortened and the success rate is increased. (1)
 Faster recovery can reduce the chance of disease transmission. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Owing to medical advances, many infectious diseases are now under control. However,
new threats such as multidrug-resistant ‘superbugs’, SARS and COVID-19 pose new
challenges to the health profession and the general public. Discuss what challenges are
faced by the health profession and how the general public should co-operate to prevent
the emergence and spread of noval diseases. (11 marks)
questions.answerText:
Challenges faced by the health profession: (Max. 4)
 The indiscriminate use of antibiotics in humans and animal rearing speeds up the
emergence of antibiotic resistance among pathogens. (1) Infections caused by
multidrug-resistant ‘superbugs’ (e.g. MRSA) are difficult to treat and if not
controlled properly they may cause an epidemic. (1)
 New strains of pathogens may emerge due to mutation, e.g. avian flu and swine flu.
(1) People do not have immunity against these new strains. Thus many people
would be infected and the transmission could be very quick. (1)
 Urbanization of formerly rural areas may bring people into contact with pathogens
from wild organisms / soil. (1) These pathogens from wild organisms / soil may
transmit to humans. (1)
 Global warming increases the incidence of some infectious diseases such as
malaria. (1)
 Frequent transport of people and goods facilitates the spread of diseases around the
world. (1)
Ways to prevent the emergence and spread of noval diseases: (Max. 4)
 When prescribed with antibiotics, patients should finish the whole course as
instructed by doctors in order to kill all the pathogens in the body. (1)
 When cases of new diseases are reported, people should actively take preventive
measures and practise good personal hygiene to protect themselves from infection.
(1)
 Avoid contact with wild organisms. (1)
 Use insect repellents and mosquito nets to avoid mosquito bites. (1) Improve
environmental hygiene to control the breeding of disease vectors (e.g. mosquitoes
and rats). (1)
 If infected with new diseases, patients should see a doctor immediately and follow
isolation order as advised by doctors. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(11 marks)

questions.text:
Avian influenza and malaria are threatening diseases transmitted through different ways.
Describe the causes and transmission routes of these diseases. Discuss what
precautionary measures can be taken to control their spread. (13 marks)
questions.answerText:
Avian influenza: (Max. 5)
 Avian influenza may be caused by several types of influenza viruses that originate
from birds, e.g. H5N1, H9N2 and H7N9. (1)
 People may catch these viruses through contact with infected birds and their
droppings. (1)
 To control the spread of avian influenza, we should
- avoid touching birds and their droppings. (1)
- cook the meat and eggs of poultry thoroughly. (1)
- wash our hands thoroughly with liquid soap and water after handling chickens
or eggs. (1)
- maintain good personal hygiene. Wash hands frequently. (1)
- consult a doctor if we have any flu-like symptoms. (1)
Malaria: (Max. 5)
 Malaria is caused by several species of the protozoan Plasmodium. (1)
 It is transmitted by the vectors mosquitoes. (1) The mosquito first bites an infected
person and takes up the protozoans. When it bites a healthy person, the protozoans
are transmitted to that person. (1)
 Malaria is not transmitted from person to person. However, malaria can be
transmitted through contaminated blood or blood product transfusion, organ
transplant, or shared needles or syringes. (1) Malaria may also be transmitted from
a mother to her foetus/newborn baby before or during delivery. (1)
 To control the spread of malaria, we should
- take measures to avoid mosquito bite, e.g. wear light-coloured, long-sleeved
clothing (1); apply effective insect repellents to exposed parts of the body and
clothing (1).
- Avoid travelling to areas where malaria is common. (1)
_________
(13 marks)

questions.text:
Lung cancer is among the top 3 commonest cancer in Hong Kong in 2017. Describe
how a malignant tumour may form in the lungs. Based on the risk factors for lung

questions.answerText:
Formation of a malignant tumour: (Max. 3)
 The genes that regulate cell division in lung cells undergo mutations. (1)
 The mutated lung cells divide uncontrollably and excessively, forming a mass of
abnormal cells called a tumour. (1)
 Mutations further accummulate in the lung cells which become cancer cells
(malignant). (1)
 The malignant tumour may spread to other parts of the body through the
bloodstream or the lymphatic system, and invade other tissues to form new
malignant tumours. (1)
Risk factors and preventive measures: (Max. 6)

(12 marks)

questions.text:
Give an account on how obesity is linked to a high risk of cardiovascular diseases.
(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Obesity caused by improper diet and lack of physical activity: (Max. 3)
 When our energy intake is greater than our energy output, the excess energy will be
stored as fat in our body and this causes weight gain. (1)
 When the body weight of a person is much greater than the normal range, the
person is described as obese. (1)
 Obesity is usually caused by high-fat and/or high-sugar diet. (1)
 Lack of physical activity also leads to obesity. (1)
Relation between a high-fat diet and cardiovascular diseases: (Max. 4)
 Eating too many foods that are rich in saturated fats or cholesterol leads to high
cholesterol content in the blood. (1)
 Excess cholesterol and other fatty substances in blood deposit on the inner walls of
coronary arteries, forming plaque. (1)
 Plaque gradually increases in size, narrowing the lumen of the coronary artery. (1)
 A blood clot may form on the surface of plaque and this may completely block the
lumen of the coronary artery. (1)
 When the coronary artery is blocked, the blood supply to the cardiac muscle
becomes inadequate. (1)
 The cardiac muscle around the blocked artery cannot obtain enough oxygen and
nutrients, and may die. (1)
Relation between insufficient physical activity and cardiovascular diseases: (Max. 2)
 When we are physically inactive, our energy output is low and we may become
overweight or obese. (1)
 Obese people are more likely to have high blood pressure. (1)
 High blood pressure may cause damage to the delicate coronary arteries. (1)
 Being overweight or obese makes the heart work harder, increasing the risk of
heart attack. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Describe and explain how the different components of blood are involved in body
defence against pathogens. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Blood clotting: (Max. 3)
 Blood platelets and fibrinogen in blood plasma are involved in blood clotting. (1)
 When a blood vessel is damaged, blood platelets are attracted to the wound by
chemicals released from the vessel wall. (1)
 The blood platelets and the damaged cells at the wound release substances that start
a series of reactions. These reactions eventually cause fibrinogen to convert into
fibrin. (1)
 The fibrin threads form a network which traps red blood cells, blood platelets and
white blood cells, forming a blood clot. (1)
Phagocytosis: (Max. 2)
 Phagocytosis involves white blood cells called phagocytes. (1)
 When a phagocyte encounter a pathogen, it encloses the pathogen in a vacuole. (1)
 Lysosome in the phagocyte fuses with the vacuole containing the pathogen and
lysozyme is released to digest the pathogen. (1)
Immune responses: (Max. 4)
 Specific immune responses involve lymphocytes: T cells and B cells. (1)
 When an antigen of a pathogen binds to a B cell with the matching receptor, the B
cell becomes activated and divides and differentiate into plasma cells and memory
B cells. (1)
 Plasma cells secrete antibodies into blood, tissue fluid and lymph to act against the
invading pathogen. (1)
 Memory B cells ‘memorize’ the antigen. They are important for the secondary
response. (1)
 When a helper T cell detects an antigen, it becomes activated and releases
chemicals called lymphokines. (1)
 Lymphokines activate other T cells to divide and differentiate into killer T cells
and memory T cells. (1)
 Killer T cells bind to the cells infected by pathogens or cancer cells and destroy
them directly. (1)
 Memory T cells ‘memorize’ the antigen. They are important for the secondary
response. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Describe and give examples about how humans acquire immunity actively and passively.
Note that details of the actions of B cells and T cells are not required. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Active immunity: (Max. 2)
 Introduction of antigens into the human body leads to immune responses (1)
 Antibody production by plasma cells is stimulated by the antigens (1)
 Formation of memory cells (1)
Natural active immunity: (1)
 Infection by pathogens, e.g. bacteria, fungi, virus, etc.
Artificial active immunity: (1)
 Vaccination; injection of weakened or killed pathogen, or its antigen
Passive immunity: (Max. 3)
 The body receives ready-made antibodies (1)
 Providing immediate protection (1)
 Immunity is short-term as the antibodies are used up (1)
 No memory cells are formed (1)
Natural passive immunity: (1)
 Antibodies transfer from a mother to a foetus across the placenta (1)
 Antibodies transfer from a mother to an infant through breast feeding (1)
Artificial passive immunity: (1)
 Injection of ready-made antibodies, e.g. serum containing high concentration of
antibodies (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_________
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Discuss the role of genetic and environmental factors in determining the colour of human
skin. (10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Genetic Factors: (Max. 5)
 Skin colour is controlled by genes that regulate the production of melanin. (1)
 Different combinations of the alleles for such genes between individuals causes
variation in skin colour. (1)
 During meiosis, the independent assortment of chromosomes leads to the formation
of gametes with different combinations of alleles that control melanin production.
(1)
 During meiosis, crossing over also produces gametes with new combinations of
alleles that control melanin production. (1)
 During fertilization, male and female gametes with different genetic makeup fuse
together randomly. This gives rise to children with different combinations of alleles
for melanin production and thus leads to different skin colour. (1)
 If mutations occur in the genes that control the production of melanin, the structure
or function of the proteins controlled by these genes may be altered. These could
lead to changes in skin colour. (1)
Environmental Factors: (Max. 2)
 Environmental factors can also affect the production of melanin in humans. (1)
 Frequent exposure to sunlight causes the human body to produce more melanin,
which results in darker skin. (1)
 Low exposure to sunlight causes the human body to produce fewer melanin, which
results in lighter skin. (1)
(Other reasonable answers)
Communication (Max. 3)
_______
(10 marks)

questions.text: Describe how DNA directs the synthesis of salivary amylase. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Transcription (Max. 4)
 An RNA polymerase molecule binds to the DNA at the beginning of the gene that
controls the production of salivary amylase. (1)
 Hydrogen bonds between the bases of the two DNA strands break and the DNA
double helix unwinds. (1)
 As the RNA polymerase molecule moves along the DNA template strand, free
RNA nucleotides are attached to the template strand through complementary base
pairing. (1)
 RNA polymerase catalyses the joining of adjacent RNA nucleotides to form an
mRNA. (1)
 Once the whole gene has been transcribed, the mRNA separates from the DNA
template strand. (1)
 The mRNA leaves the nucleus through the nuclear pores and enters the cytoplasm.
(1)
Translation (Max. 5)
 The mRNA binds to a ribosome in the cytoplasm. (1)
 Each tRNA molecule with a particular anticodon only carries a specific amino acid.
(1)
 tRNA with anticodons complementary to the codons of the mRNA will attach to
the ribosome. (1)
 Adjacent amino acids are joined together by peptide bonds. (1)
 The ribosome moves one codon at a time down the mRNA, adding one amino acid
at a time to the growing polypeptide chain. (1)
 When the ribosome reaches a stop codon, the translation process is complete and
the polypeptide formed is released from the ribosome. (1)
 The polypeptide coils and folds to form the protein salivary amylase. (1)
Communication (Max. 3)
_______
(12 marks)

questions.text:
Discuss, with examples, how biotechnology contributes to different aspects of medicine.
Briefly explain the working principles of the techniques involved.
(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Diagnosis of genetic diseases (Max.4)
 DNA fingerprinting is used to diagnose genetic diseases in both prenatal and
newborn babies. These diseases may include cystic fibrosis, haemophilia,
Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, sickle-cell anaemia and thalassemia. (1)
 DNA fingerprinting is a technique for finding unique patterns in a person’s DNA.
(1) By comparing large groups of people with and without a particular genetic
disease, it is possible to identify DNA patterns associated with the disease. (1)

fossils as evidence for evolution. (12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Fossils as evidence for evolution: (6)

the past. (1)

existence, we can observe how organisms changed over time. (1)

molecule. (1)

 All organisms use the same 20 types of amino acids to synthesize proteins as

 Certain essential proteins are commonly found in many different organisms. Their
amino acid sequences may be slightly different as a result of mutations. (1)
 The amino acid sequences of essential proteins in different organisms can be
compared to deduce the evolutionary relationship among them. (1)
 Scientists assume that the fewer the number of amino acid differences of a protein

questions.text:

 Plants usually produce huge amounts of pollen / seeds. (1)

stomach acid induced by stress. However, many patients developed gastric ulcer again
after being treated with medicines for neutralizing stomach acid. In the 1980s, the

bacterium called Helicobacter pylori in their stomach. He therefore put forward a

(a) Suggest the hypothesis made by Marshall about gastric ulcer. (1 mark)

Scientists study how Helicobacter pylori survives in the stomach. To avoid the acidic
environment of the stomach, H. pylori uses its flagella to burrow into the mucus lining
of the stomach to reach the epithelial cells underneath, where it is less acidic. H. pylori
is able to detect the pH gradient in the mucus and move towards the less acidic region.
(d) Give two characteristics of organisms demonstrated by Helicobacter pylori in the
passage above. (2 marks)
(e) Elaborate on how the events above demonstrate the following aspect of the nature
of science: Scientific knowledge is tentative and subject to change. (2 marks)

(b) Introduce Helicobacter pylori into the stomach of healthy mammals. (1)

survival of bacteria. (1)
(d) Movement, sensitivity (1, 1)
(e) Barry Marshall’s new findings provide evidence that gastric ulcer is caused by
Helicobacter pylori. (1)
His findings corrected the previous misconception that gastric ulcer was caused by
excessive secretion of stomach acid. (1)

(8 marks)

Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.
Water intoxication
An American woman joined a water-drinking contest. However, she found
her head painful and was later found dead in her house. Coroner inquest had
shown that her death was related to water intoxication.
Water is essential to our bodies, but drinking too much water will cause the
brain to swell. This prevents the brain from regulating vital functions and is
lethal. However, our bodies can regulate the water content in the body and the
water potential of the blood. If we drink too much water, the kidneys will be
unable to work fast enough to excrete the excess water, so the blood becomes

(b) Drinking too much water will dilute the blood. (1)
This will lead to a net movement of water molecules from the blood to the body
cells and cause the cells to burst. (1)
(c) (i) urination (1)
sweating (1)
(ii) Urination and sweating can remove excess water from the body. (1)
The blood will become less dilute and its water potential decreases / returns to
normal level. (1)

of pineapple jelly for a party. However, the jelly solution failed to coagulate and
remained in the liquid state even after it had cooled down.
She then searched for information on the Internet and found that jelly would become a
semi-solid when the protein molecules inside formed bonded with each other.
(a) Which enzyme does fresh pineapple contain that prevents the jelly solution from
solidifying? Explain how it worked. (3 marks)
(b) State two characteristics of the enzyme answered in (a). (2 marks)
(c) Wendy’s classmate suggested that she should use canned pineapple instead of fresh
pineapple, so that the jelly solution mixed with the pineapple can coagulate
successfully. Comment on this method. (Hint: What treatment is applied in making
canned pineapple?) (3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a) Protease (1)
The protease from the fresh pineapple breaks down the bonds formed between the
protein molecules in the jelly solution. (1)
In the absence of bonds that hold the protein molecules in a regular pattern, the
jelly cannot turn from the liquid state into a semi-solid. (1)
(b) Any two of the following: (2)
 They are biological catalysts. (1)
 They are specific in action. (1)
 They are reusable. (1)

(Or other reasonable answers)
(c) Pineapple is treated at a high temperature during the canning process. (1)
The proteases are denatured at the high temperature and (1)
they could not break the bonds formed between the protein molecules in the jelly
solution. (1)
Therefore the jelly is able to solidify.
________
(8 marks)

questions.text:
Before the discovery of vitamins, scientists had been suspecting that some foods (e.g.
milk) contain certain factors essential to good health and humans require only small
amounts of these factors.
The table below shows some investigations carried out by two scientists on the
‘essential factors’ in milk.
Scientist Wilhelm Stepp (1882‒1964)
Hypothesis The essential factor(s) in milk might be associated with lipids.
Treatment He mixed flour with milk to make ‘milk bread’. He added alcohol
and ether to the milk bread to extract the essential factor.
Experimental group:
The mice were fed with the treated milk bread only.
Control group:
The mice were fed with the treated milk bread and the extract.
Observation Experimental group:
All the mice died within three weeks.
Control group:
All survived normally after three weeks.
Scientist Frederick Hopkins (1861‒1947)
Hypothesis Milk contains some ‘accessory factors’ which are essential for the
healthy growth of young rats.
Treatment He fed two groups of young rats with proteins, lipids,
carbohydrates and minerals. He gave milk to one group only. After
two weeks, he switched to feed the second group with milk.
Observation When the mice were fed with milk, they grew normally. When the
mice lacked milk, they did not grow well.
(a) Why did Stepp extract the essential factor in milk bread with alcohol and
ether? (1 mark)
(b) Did the results of Stepp’s experiment support his hypothesis? (3 marks)
(c) What conclusion can be drawn from Hopkins’ experiment? (1 mark)
(d) Elaborate on one aspect about the nature of science that can be demonstrated in the
above events. (2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a) He believed that the essential factor was associated with lipids, and that it would
dissolve in organic solvents such as alcohol and ether. (1)
(b) Yes. (1)
The group fed with the treated milk bread only did not receive the essential factor
and they died. (1)
The group fed with the extract survived normally. This shows that the essential
factor dissolved in the alcohol and ether. (1)
(c) Milk contains some ‘accessory factors’ which are essential for the healthy growth
of young rats. (1)
(d) Inquiry procedures are guided by the hypotheses made.
Stepp and Hopkins made different hypotheses. They treated the mice differently
based on their own hypothesis. (1) + (1)
OR
Different investigative procedures may come to the same conclusions.
Stepp and Hopkins carried out different experiments, but they both reached the
conclusion that milk contains some essential substances that are important for
growth. (1) + (1)
OR
A good scientific experiment must include carefully designed controls.
Stepp and Hopkins both had set up experimental group and control group which
differed only in the factor under investigation. (1) + (1)
(Or other reasonable answers)
_________
(7 marks)

questions.text:
Jonathan consulted a nutritionist and was told that he has obesity. The doctor advised
him to make changes to his diet and increase his daily energy expenditure. The table
below shows the activities and the relative energy intake or consumption of Jonathan in
a day.
Activity Energy (kJ)
Breakfast 3500
Walk to school 2000
Lunch 4000
Do homework 3000
Play TV game 1500
Dinner 6000
Watch TV 1000
(a) Calculate the difference between energy input and energy output of Jonathan for
one day. Explain why Jonathan has obesity. (5 marks)
(b) Jonathan searched a diet called ‘lean meats diet’, which encourages people to
consume lean meats only in their diet. Jonathan thought that this diet could
effectively reduce his weight.
If you were Jonathan’s doctor, explain the advantages and disadvantages of this
diet. (4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a) Energy input = 3500 + 4000 + 6000 =13500 kJ (1)
Energy output = 2000 + 3000 + 1500 + 1000 = 7500 kJ (1)
Difference between energy input and output = 13500 – 7500 = 6000 kJ (1)
The energy intake of his diet is much greater than the energy output of the body, (1)
so the excess energy is stored as fats in the body. (1)
(b) Advantages: (Any two, 2)
 Lean meats do not contain fats and carbohydrates, hence reducing his energy
intake. (1)
 Lean meats are rich in proteins, which helps build muscles for his growth and
development. (1)
 Lean meats contain a low level of cholesterol, which does not incur heart
diseases or high blood pressure. (1)
(Or other reasonable answers)
Disadvantages: (Any two, 2)
 Omission of essential nutrients, such as vitamins and minerals in the diet may
incur health problems (1)
 Omission of dietary fiber in the diet may incur constipation. (1)
(Or other reasonable answers)
________
(9 marks)

(g) (g) (g) fibre (g)

questions.text:
Many fruits are rich in vitamin C. The vitamin C content of fruit often decreases during
storage.
(a) A freshly-picked orange is found to contain 100 mg of vitamin C. Another
similar-sized orange was stored for two weeks and is found to contain 73 mg of
vitamin C.
Calculate the percentage decrease in vitamin C content of orange after storage of
two weeks. (2 marks)
(b) (i) State two properties of vitamin C which lead to the loss of vitamin C during
the storage of fruits. (2 marks)
(ii) According to the properties of vitamin C, suggest two ways to reduce the loss
of vitamin C during storage. (2 marks)
(c) (i) What is the deficiency disease of vitamin C? (1 mark)
(ii) Explain how a lack of vitamin C causes this disease. (2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a) Decrease in vitamin C content = 73 mg – 100 mg = –27 mg (1)
Percentage decrease in vitamin C content = (–27 mg / 100 mg) × 100% = –27% (1)
(b) (i) Vitamin C is easily oxidized by oxygen in the air. (1)
Vitamin C is destroyed at higher temperatures. (1)
(ii) Any two of the following: (2)
 storage with low oxygen
 coating with wax (to reduce oxygen entry)
 keeping in a cool environment
(Or other reasonable answer)
(c) (i) scurvy (1)
(ii) Vitamin C is needed in the formation of connective tissues. (1)
A lack of vitamin C will lead to bleeding gums / poor healing of wounds. (1)
________
(9 marks)

questions.text:
Vitamins and minerals are important to our health.
(a) Give two similarities and two differences between vitamins and minerals. (4 marks)
(b) Which vitamin and mineral are essential for bone formation? (2 marks)
(c) Which pigment are carrots rich in? State the importance of this pigment to the
human body. (3 marks)
(d) Anaemia is a disease of iron deficiency. The symptoms of anaemia include feeling
tired easily and fainting. Explain why the deficiency of iron would lead to these
symptoms. (3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a) Similarities:
Both provide no energy to the human body. (1)
Both are needed in very small amounts for maintaining good health. (1)
(Or other reasonable answer)
Differences: (Any two, 2)
 Vitamins are organic substances while minerals are inorganic.
 Some types of vitamins (e.g. vitamin D) can be synthesized by the human
body, but minerals cannot be synthesized by the human body.
 Some types of vitamins are water-soluble and some are lipid-soluble.
Minerals are not soluble in lipids.
(Or other reasonable answer)
(b) vitamin D (1)
calcium (1)
(c) carotene (1)
Carotene can be converted to vitamin A. (1)
Vitamin A is needed for the formation of visual purple, the pigment responsible for
night vision. (1)
(d) Iron is a component of haemoglobin, (1)
which is the oxygen-carrying pigment in red blood cells. (1)
A lack of iron would lead to inadequate oxygen supply to body parts, including the
brain. (1)

questions.text:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.
Low-alcohol beer
The market for low-alcohol beer in the United States is experiencing great
growth due to the demand for healthy drinks, the increased concern over the social
effects of excessive alcohol consumption and drunk-driving legislation. There are
two approaches in producing low-alcohol beer: physical treatment of the beer and
adaptation of the existing brewing process.
Physical treatment involves passing beer that is under high pressure through a
reactor with a selectively permeable membrane. Alcohol and water molecules can
pass through the membrane more readily than the larger molecules in the beer.
Additional water is then added to the filtered beer to dilute it, thus producing the
low-alcohol beer.
In comparison, adaptation of the existing brewing process can prevent too
much alcohol from being produced in the first place. There are three methods to
achieve this:
(a) Chill the yeast before fermentation
(b) Use fewer carbohydrates
(c) Create a new strain of yeast that converts fewer carbohydrates to alcohol
Some scientists believe that the third method is the most promising. They hope
the new strain of yeast can be used to make a healthy and driver-friendly beer that
does not differ greatly in taste.
(a) Why is high pressure applied to the beer in the physical treatment? (1 mark)
(b) Explain why the following methods can reduce the production of alcohol in yeast.
(i) Chilling the yeast before fermentation (2 marks)
(ii) Using fewer carbohydrates (2 marks)
(c) Name the technology that can be used to create the new strain of yeast. (1 mark)
(d) State one example of the following benefits that low-alcohol beer can bring:
(i) social benefits (1 mark)
(ii) health benefits (1 mark)
questions.answerText:
(a) The high pressure increases the rate of movement of water and alcohol across the
selectively permeable membrane. (1)
(b) (i) Alcoholic fermentation is catalysed by yeast enzymes. (1)
Low temperatures inactivate these enzymes and inhibit the fermentation. (1)
(ii) Carbohydrates are the substrate in alcoholic fermentation. (1)
The rate of reaction is limited by the concentration of substrates, so the rate of
the fermentation can be lowered by reducing the amount of carbohydrates
used. (1)
(c) Genetic engineering / recombinant DNA technology (1)
(d) (i) The number of traffic accidents caused by drunk-driving will be reduced. (1)
(Or other reasonable answers)
(ii) Liver damage caused by alcohol will be reduced. (1)
(Or other reasonable answers)
________
(8 marks)

questions.text:
Infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) are difficult
to treat because these bacteria are resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin,
amoxicillin and methicillin. Some strains of S. aureus produce beta-lactamase, an
enzyme that breaks the structures of beta-lactam antibiotics.
(a) Beta-lactam antibiotics are bactericidal and act by inhibiting the synthesis of the
peptidoglycan layer of bacterial cell walls. Explain how these antibiotics kill non-
resistant bacteria. (3 marks)
(b) Describe how the indiscriminate use of antibiotics may have speeded up the
development of antibiotic resistance in a population of Staphylococcus aureus.
(4 marks)
(c) Using your knowledge about enzymes, suggest how antibiotic treatments for
MRSA can be made effective again. (2 marks)
